full_text:
**Verdict: KNOWN.** I'm changing the first pass's KNOWN-VARIANT to KNOWN. The only observed feature, "cells flip back and forth," is standard behaviour of spatial evolutionary games where each cell copies its best-scoring neighbour (the Nowak–May family). There is no twist in what the system actually does, so "variant" isn't justified.

**What the system is.** Two strategies sit on a lattice. Each cell copies its best-scoring neighbour, and only 10% of cells update each step (p=0.1). This is the Nowak–May spatial game. Payoffs were accumulated in every generation, and every player chose the strategy of his neighbor with the highest payoff as his strategy in the next generation. The rule is literally named "unconditional imitation (Nowak and May's model)" in a standard review, which covers both Prisoner's Dilemma (40) and Snowdrift games (41). So it doesn't matter whether g=(1.5, 0.5) is read as a Prisoner's Dilemma or a Snowdrift game. Updating only 10% of cells per step is a known variant too; studies routinely compare asynchronous versus synchronous updating.

**Why the flipping is documented.** Persistent strategy changes at the boundaries between cooperator and defector clusters are the defining behaviour of this model. Nowak–May describe dynamic fractal patterns and transient chaos. Later work found the system settles into a state with a few periodic patterns; periodic patterns mean individual cells reverse their strategy over and over. Work on asynchronous updating also describes occasional strategy flippings that are quickly undone, which is the same back-and-forth behaviour.

**Genuine or trivial?** The flipping isn't a numerical artifact, but it says very little:
- **The knock-out comparison is close to meaningless.** Copying the best neighbour is the only rule in the system. Removing every rule that reads neighbours leaves nothing that can change a cell, so the knock-out is frozen and has zero reversals by construction. A difference of 1.0 versus 0.0 only shows that the dynamics are not frozen.
- **The measure looks maxed out.** A median of exactly 1.0 with a spread of 0.02 suggests g_reversals is effectively a yes/no flag for "some reversals occur." It doesn't show any distinctive spatial or time structure.
- **A frozen state is plausible but didn't happen here.** Asynchronous updating can push these models toward frozen states (Huberman & Glance 1993; I'm citing this from memory, not from the search). The measurements show the run didn't freeze, which fits the coexistence regime of these games.

I ran one search covering Nowak–May, asynchronous updating, unconditional imitation and fluctuation behaviour. Its results were enough to place both the model and the behaviour.
